journeys.title: Silk Road by train

books.title: Across the American South
books.dek: A train route of vinegar, mustard, pepper, and Gulf sauces.
intro: Southern barbecue is a map. Eastern North Carolina is vinegar and pepper. Lexington adds a little tomato. The South Carolina Midlands use mustard. Alabama’s white sauce is mayonnaise. Memphis is a thinner tomato sauce.

Enslaved West African cooks and their descendants shaped Southern pits and pepper sauces. English and Scottish settlers brought vinegar habits. German settlement in the Midlands is the usual account of the mustard sauce. This book follows that route and does not pretend one gravy belongs to one people only.

books.title: Appalachian Sauces
books.dek: Biscuit gravies, sorghum, and chow-chow from the upland South.
intro: Appalachian sauces in this book are the ones that can be tied to a real pot: red-eye gravy, sausage gravy (sometimes called sawmill gravy), chocolate gravy, tomato gravy, sorghum glaze, and chow-chow.

Scots-Irish and English settlers brought biscuit and vinegar habits into the mountains in the eighteenth century. German-speaking settlers, often by way of Pennsylvania, brought sweet-sour pickling. Enslaved people and later Black Appalachian cooks worked the same farms and kitchens. Their labor is part of this food, not a footnote.

Cherokee and other Native nations of these mountains grew corn and foraged long before those settlements. This book does not assign chocolate gravy, chow-chow, or sorghum glaze to them. Those recipes are later mountain home cooking. No Cherokee sauce is invented here to fill a gap.

books.title: Pasta Sauces
books.dek: From a Roman cheese-and-pepper emulsion to a Bolognese ragù.
intro: Italian pasta sauces are often named for a city or a method: cacio e pepe, amatriciana, pesto alla Genovese, ragù alla Bolognese. Italian-American kitchens added Sunday gravy and vodka sauce. This book keeps those histories separate.
Print the booklet for a sauce-by-sauce comparison. The field-guide page for each sauce has the longer origin note.

intro: A marinade seasons the surface and, when it contains acid or salt, changes texture. It is still a sauce: you can boil the leftover marinade if it has touched raw meat, or reserve a portion before it does.

books.title: The Mother Sauces & Their Children
books.dek: The five French mother sauces and the named sauces built from them, plus a few classics from other kitchens.
intro: In the French system taught since the nineteenth century, five mother sauces anchor a repertoire: béchamel, velouté, espagnole, sauce tomate, and hollandaise. Mayonnaise, béarnaise, and a vinaigrette sit beside them as emulsions.

A mother sauce is a method, not a claim that other cultures descend from Paris. Mole, pesto, and nuoc cham are in this book because they are classics of their own kitchens, not because they are French daughters.

passages.title: Across the American South
passages.text: Enslaved West African cooks and their descendants shaped Southern pits and pepper sauces. English and Scottish settlers brought vinegar habits. German settlement in the Midlands is the usual account of the mustard sauce. This book follows that route and does not pretend one gravy belongs to one people only.
passages.label: From the book

passages.title: Appalachian Sauces
passages.text: Scots-Irish and English settlers brought biscuit and vinegar habits into the mountains in the eighteenth century. German-speaking settlers, often by way of Pennsylvania, brought sweet-sour pickling. Enslaved people and later Black Appalachian cooks worked the same farms and kitchens. Their labor is part of this food, not a footnote.
passages.label: From the book

passages.title: Cajun & Creole Louisiana
passages.text: Creole cooking in New Orleans drew on French and Spanish colonial kitchens, West African cooking carried by enslaved people, Caribbean links, and Native American ingredients such as filé. Cajun cooking grew among Acadian exiles in rural southwest Louisiana. The usual distinction is city tomato and butter against a darker rural roux. It is a useful distinction, not a wall.
passages.label: From the book

passages.title: New England Shore
passages.text: English Puritan settlers in the seventeenth century met a cold coast: dairy, cod, lobster, and native cranberry bogs already used by Wampanoag and other Native people. Drawn butter and cranberry sauce are the shore sauces in this guide.
passages.label: From the book

passages.title: Salsa Veracruzana
passages.text: Salsa veracruzana is the tomato sauce of Veracruz for fish, with olive, caper, and often bay and thyme. Those Mediterranean pantry items arrived with Spanish colonial trade and stayed in the Gulf kitchen. The sauce is cooked and spooned over fish.
passages.label: From the field guide

passages.title: Hot Bacon Dressing
passages.text: Hot bacon dressing is the Pennsylvania Dutch dressing for wilted lettuce, dandelion, or spinach. Bacon fat, vinegar, and sugar are warmed and poured over the greens so they soften. Pennsylvania Dutch means the German-speaking settlers of Pennsylvania, from Deutsch, not the Netherlands. The dressing is a home sauce of that community.
passages.label: From the field guide

passages.title: Mango Chutney
passages.text: Cooked mango chutney is an Indian preserve that British cooks adopted in the colonial period and sweetened into the jar now common with cheese and cold meat. Major Grey’s is a brand style, not a single historic recipe. This is a home cooked mango chutney with ginger and chile, for the refrigerator, not a canning formula.
